title: Kentucky River Palisades
summary: For about a hundred miles through the Inner Bluegrass, the Kentucky River cuts deep meanders into hard Ordovician limestone, forming the Palisades.
bodyMarkdown:
For about 100 miles through the Inner Bluegrass, the [Kentucky River Palisades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_River_Palisades) line the river with steep limestone walls. The cliffs [rise as high as 250 feet](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky_River) above the water along stretches in Jessamine, Garrard and Madison counties.

## How the gorge formed

The river's bends are entrenched meanders. They first took shape as the stream wandered across the gently rolling Lexington Peneplain. During the Quaternary period, base level fell and the river cut straight down, locking those old loops into a deep gorge.

The rocks are Ordovician in age. Softer Lexington Limestone weathers into gentle slopes. Beneath it, the harder High Bridge Group, made up of the Tyrone, Oregon and Camp Nelson formations, holds the vertical cliffs.

## The fault

The Kentucky River Fault crosses the area. Movement along it was largely vertical, raising the land on the north side by several hundred feet. That uplift brought resistant rock into the river's path.

When the downcutting river reached the Camp Nelson rocks, its old meanders hardened into the curving cliffs seen today. Fort Boonesborough stood near the fault and near the eastern end of the palisades.

## River travel

Early settlers used the river mainly to float goods and emigrants downstream on flatboats. [Rocky shoals in stretches like the Palisades](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky_River), along with snags and low water, caused frequent groundings. Those hazards made upstream keelboat travel slow and difficult. A system of 14 locks and dams later enabled commercial navigation. It still regulates the water level for flood control and steady flow.

## A refuge for plants and animals

The cliffs shelter the largest concentration of forest left in the Inner Bluegrass. Blue ash, chinquapin oak, sugar maple, rock elm and yellowwood grow on the slopes. In spring, the woods fill with ephemeral wildflowers. Four endangered bat species live in the area.

## Kentucky today

In 2007 the state [bought 90 acres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_River_Palisades) next to Tom Dorman State Nature Preserve, adding to the protected land along the cliffs. The river below the palisades now [supplies drinking water](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kentucky_River) to more than 600,000 people through 68 public utilities. Its watershed covers about 7,000 square miles across 42 counties. The Palisades are counted as its defining physical feature.
